definition: The FAA rule against interfering with a crewmember, which the agency uses for civil penalties in laser cases.
The US federal crime of knowingly aiming a laser pointer at an aircraft or its flight path, punishable by up to five years in prison and a fine.
FDA permission to market a device because it is substantially equivalent to one already on the market.
Non-representational moving laser patterns.
A deformable mirror that reshapes itself about 1000 times a second to cancel atmospheric blur.
Lasers set up to throw beams into the sky as a landmark, as at Coachella's Quasar stage in 2025.
Automatic identification and data capture, such as a 2D code.
US Boeing 747-based missile-defense laser test aircraft, tested at Edwards Air Force Base from 2002 and retired to storage in 2012.
Continuous brightness control of each laser, usually 256 steps per color.
Repeated points at a line end or corner that give the scanners time to stop or turn.
The US voluntary consensus standard for safe laser use, which OSHA cites as guidance.
A gas laser with strong blue and green lines, first seen working on February 14, 1964. The bright beam of 1970s rock tours.
A network transport for DMX lighting control data.

term: Assignment for the Benefit of Creditors (ABC)
definition: A state-law alternative to bankruptcy, used by Glowforge in 2025.
Gas blown down a cutting nozzle: oxygen adds heat by burning the metal, nitrogen only blows out the melt.
Beams deliberately swept through the crowd at levels meant to stay within the exposure limit. Excluded by the standard conditions of a US variance.
A laser show run from recorded control tracks, with nobody playing it. Lovelight (1977) is described as the first.
The blink or turn-away reflex to bright light. Exposure limits for visible beams assume it takes 0.25 seconds.
A 64 by 64 brightness map over a zone that dims or blocks output in chosen areas (Pangolin's term).
A show seen in mid-air: shapes scanned through haze as beams, fans, cones and tunnels.
A row of actuators that switch the beam to fixed positions, each aimed at a bounce mirror.
Ending a beam on a surface so it goes no farther into the sky or the crowd.
Pangolin's laser show control software, named in most festival case studies.
Switching the beam off while the scanners move between parts of an image.
The early powered flight of a missile, when the Airborne Laser was designed to engage it.
The US Food and Drug Administration unit that inspected laser light shows in the late 1970s.
A metal link joining battery cells into modules and packs, often laser welded.
Running cues live to the music instead of playing back a time-coded show.
The FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health, which receives laser product reports and variance applications.
Stretching a light pulse, amplifying it, then compressing it again; the subject of half the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Above 5 mW up to 500 mW. Hazardous even for brief accidental direct exposure.
Up to 5 mW of visible output; the most a US show projector may emit without an FDA variance.
Above 500 mW. An eye and skin hazard from the direct or reflected beam, and often a fire hazard.
Visible output up to 5 mW; the US ceiling for laser pointers and for show projectors without a variance.
Output from 5 to 500 mW; in the US it cannot legally be promoted as a laser pointer or demonstration laser.
The class above IIIb; US show projectors in this class need an FDA variance.
A scanner whose position detector feeds a servo amplifier that corrects the mirror.
Light waves staying in step in phase, because each stimulated photon copies the one that triggered it.
Chemical oxygen iodine laser, the megawatt-class laser carried by the Airborne Laser.
The doctor a Texas laser hair removal facility must have a written contract with.
Laser output that is steady over time rather than pulsed.
A gas laser used on large 1990s tours; Pink Floyd's 1994 US tour carried two 50 W systems.
A three-mirror prism that sends light straight back where it came from; Apollo 11's panel holds 100 of them.
The operating cost of one laser engagement, the main argument governments make for laser weapons.
FAA airspace within 10 NM of an airport up to 10,000 ft above ground, capped in Advisory Circular 70-1B at 5 microwatts/cm2.
Digital-to-analog converter: the hardware that turns software output into the voltages a projector takes.
A visible laser meant to cause temporary, reversible glare, used as a warning at checkpoints and at sea.
A formal diplomatic protest.
The US legal term for a laser made, designed, intended or promoted for demonstration, entertainment, advertising display or artistic composition.
A mirror or filter that passes one color and reflects others; used to merge red, green and blue into one beam.
A ruled sheet that splits one beam into a fan of many. The Who's 1975 effect used a hand-held one.
The smallest spot a lens can focus light into, set by the wavelength.
A semiconductor chip that lases when current is applied to it, with no crystal in between.
A weapon that uses focused energy, such as a laser or microwaves, instead of a projectile.
How fast a beam widens as it travels. Doubling it halves the hazard distance.
Diode-pumped solid state: an 808 nm diode pumps a crystal lasing at 1064 nm, which a second crystal doubles to 532 nm green.
UK laser weapon led by MBDA UK, due on a Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer by 2027.
Detention without physical examination: holding an import at the port because its firm is on an FDA import alert's list.
A stretch of fiber laced with erbium and pumped by a laser at 980 or 1480 nm, which boosts 1550 nm signals without turning them into electronics.
The higher-class laser inside a Class 1 enclosed product; its class applies during service.
One of the fixed amounts of energy an atom or molecule can hold; the lowest is the ground state.
Extreme ultraviolet lithography light at 13.5 nm, made by hitting tin droplets with a laser.
An ultraviolet gas laser that removes tissue in very thin layers with little heat; the laser behind PRK and LASIK.
Melting and recrystallizing amorphous silicon with an excimer line beam to make low-temperature polysilicon.
Pangolin's networked laser control hardware.
A laser whose pulses last quadrillionths of a second, used to cut corneal flaps or lenticules.
ILDA's award for technical achievement.
A solid-state laser whose gain medium is a doped optical fiber; it outsold CO2 for cutting from 2015.
Laser cutting with oxygen assist, which adds heat through an exothermic reaction.
Visible strobing when a frame has so many points that it is redrawn too few times a second.
A thicker, billowing mist that shows swirls inside the beams.
The FAA's Notice of Proposed Outdoor Laser Operation(s), filed at least 30 days before an outdoor show.
Treating skin in a grid of tiny columns, leaving untreated skin between them to speed healing.
One complete list of points for one image; frames played in sequence make animation.
A US court hearing on whether a scientific method is generally accepted before evidence from it is admitted.
Cutting by melting the metal and blowing the melt out with inert gas such as nitrogen.
The material where amplification happens: a gas, crystal, dye, fiber or semiconductor.
Galvanometer scanner: a limited-rotation motor with a small mirror on its shaft. Two of them aim the beam.
Warping the output with sliders or a mesh so shapes land correctly on the target.
Dramatic performance rights - music used to tell a story, as in opera or musical theater. They are negotiated directly with the rights holder and are outside a blanket license.
A show in which the laser draws logos, text and animation on a surface.
A bent copper bar in an e-motor stator, laser welded at its ends.
A very fine, evenly spread mist that makes beams visible as smooth cones and sheets.
High-Energy Laser with Integrated Optical Dazzler and Surveillance, a Lockheed Martin system delivered to USS Preble in 2022.
A low-power gas laser. Its red 632.8 nm line, found in 1962, gave the first continuous visible beam sold commercially.
Military term for a laser weapon meant to damage a target.
Hot isostatic pressing, used after metal printing to close internal pores.
The centimeter-sized gold cylinder at NIF that turns laser light into x-rays to squeeze the fuel capsule.
A recording of the full wavefield of light that replays a true 3D image when lit by a laser.

ILDA Accredited Professional Lasershow Company: an industry credential requiring documented shows, client references, a staff member who has passed a Laser Safety Officer course and a signed safety affirmation.
ILDA Digital Network, a protocol for streaming laser graphics, effects and DMX data over a network.
ILDA Image Data Transfer Format, for exchanging laser show frames and files between systems.
A fusion shot that releases more energy than the laser energy delivered to the target.
The International Laser Display Association, the laser show trade body.
The laser display industry's annual prizes, with artistic categories such as Beams/Atmospherics, Graphics, Planetarium and Live Stage.
A standard frame, including a circle in a square, used to tune scanners and blanking at 12,000 or 30,000 points per second.
An FDA instruction that lets border staff detain listed firms' products without examining them; Import Alert 95-04 covers laser pointers and light show projectors.
FDA import alert that lets US ports detain listed firms' laser pointers, projectors, toys and similar products without physical examination.
The UK HSE leaflet on display lasers, which puts the duty on the organizer and points to PLASA's guidance.
A laser beam carrying data between satellites.
An argon or krypton gas laser; the professional show source before solid state, water-cooled and about 0.05% efficient.
Israel's high-power laser air defense, developed by Rafael with a laser from Elbit Systems; declared operational in 2025.
Power spread over an area, in mW/cm2. It falls with distance as a beam widens.
The 25-pin analog connection carrying X, Y, color, shutter and interlock signals to a projector.
The slot a laser cut leaves.
EDC Las Vegas's main stage.
Thousands of points per second, the scanner speed rating.
A gas laser that can give red, yellow, green and blue at once. Laserium split one krypton beam into four colors with prisms.
Laserists showing off their work to each other. First recorded on August 14, 1986.
Light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation; the acronym is first recorded in Gordon Gould's November 1957 notebook.
Ablating a coating or surface layer with very brief high-power pulses, without chemicals or contact.
The unit Guinness counts for its largest laser show record: each point where a beam leaves a device, with a beam split by diffraction counted once.
The usual name for a planetarium laser show set to Pink Floyd, most often Dark Side of the Moon or The Wall. Several companies have made their own.
FAA airspace closest to runways, where visible laser light is capped at 50 nW/cm2.
An artificial star made by a laser exciting sodium atoms about 90 km up, used to correct telescope blur.
An instrument made of upright laser beams. Breaking a beam with the hand triggers a note.
ILDA's live laser performance competition.
Laser outlines fitted to the features of a building or 3D object.
UK law making it an offense to shine a laser at a vehicle that is moving or ready to move where it dazzles or distracts the person in control.
A numbered FDA guidance letter to the laser industry, such as Notice 51 on projector sales or Notice 55 on variance renewal.
FDA guidance (February 2023 version) saying the agency does not intend to enforce matching US requirements for products conforming to identified IEC 60825-1 Ed. 3 and IEC 60601-2-22 Ed. 3.1 clauses.
FDA policy letting makers certify to parts of IEC 60825-1 Ed. 3; it replaced Notice 50 at the end of 2024.
The US federal rule for laser products at 21 CFR 1040.10 and 1040.11, first published as a final rule in 1975.
Damage to the center of the retina from looking into a handheld laser.
Building a metal part by melting thin layers of powder with a laser; also called DMLM, DMLS or SLM.
Damage to the retina from laser exposure.
The named person responsible for laser safety at a facility or show. Required by name in several US states and in Germany.
The FAA flight zone near runways where outdoor laser light must stay at or below 50 nW/cm2.
A bomb that steers toward a spot of laser light placed on a target; first combat-evaluated by the US Air Force in 1968.
A video projector in which blue laser diodes light a spinning phosphor wheel and an imaging chip forms the picture; no beam is scanned.
The person who performs or operates a laser show; in the analog era, the player of the console.
The laser show Ivan Dryer opened at Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles on November 19, 1973, played live to recorded music; it ran there until January 2002.
Laserium's analog performance console, with more than 150 controls for image size, motor speeds, brightness, shape and color, by one former laserist's count.
Laserium's first all-rock program, from 1977, and the start of the rock-album planetarium format.
Germany's laser safety officer, appointed in writing before Class 3R, 3B or 4 lasers are operated by an employer who lacks the required expertise personally.
An excimer laser reshapes the cornea under a thin flap that is then laid back down. The word was coined in 1991.
Service slang for shining a laser at an aircraft or ship.
Laser Weapon System, the US Navy prototype that operated on USS Ponce in the Persian Gulf in 2014.
The FAA's reply to a notice of an outdoor laser operation, stating an objection or no objection.
Light detection and ranging: measuring distance by timing laser pulses.
A hand-held laser speed gun used in traffic enforcement, such as the LTI Marksman 20-20 a New Jersey court examined in 1998.
Haze or fog visibly swirling inside a flat sheet of scanned laser light.
A laser fiber inside the body heats and destroys tissue while MRI tracks the temperature.
A wavelength whose round trip fits the cavity a whole number of times, and so can build up.
Low-power red or near-infrared light meant to stimulate tissue rather than cut it, as in hair-growth caps and combs; also called photobiomodulation.
Low-temperature polysilicon, the faster transistor material in AMOLED phone displays.
A soft, gauze-like moving pattern made by sending a beam through rippled glass or plastic.
Microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation; the microwave forerunner of the laser, named in April 1954.
Metal plates at the aperture that cut off any output below or outside a set line, whatever the software sends.
The highest level of laser light a standard treats as acceptable for an eye or skin over a given time. For a visible beam and a quarter second it is about 2.5 mW/cm2.
FDA's voluntary system for reporting problems with medical products.
An instrument that splits a laser beam down two arms and recombines it, so tiny changes in length show up as light. The core of LIGO.
Locking a cavity's modes in phase so they add into a train of picosecond or femtosecond pulses.
Using a laser to open the clouded lens capsule after cataract surgery.
The distance at which a direct beam has spread enough for its irradiance to fall to the MPE.
A notice to aircrews. The UK CAA normally issues one for a notified outdoor laser display.
How wide a cone of light a lens gathers. A higher value focuses a smaller spot; Blu-ray uses 0.85.
Optically pumped semiconductor laser: diodes pump a thin gain chip in a small cavity, giving a clean, narrow beam and chosen colors such as 577 nm yellow.
A clock that holds atoms in a grid of laser light and probes them with a clock laser at an optical frequency.
Schawlow and Townes' term for the laser.
Crossed pairs of laser beams that slow atoms as if they were moving through syrup.
A focused laser beam that holds tiny particles and living cells; the subject of half the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The partly reflective mirror the beam leaves through.
Professional Audience Safety System, the hardware used on projectors approved to scan audiences, used on selected units at Coachella 2025.
The US family of laser-guided bomb kits adopted after the BOLT-117 evaluation in the Vietnam War.
Polychromatic acousto-optic modulator: a tellurium dioxide crystal driven by radio-frequency signals that set color and brightness on gas lasers.
A reflection illusion using a slanted transparent sheet; the method behind stage "holograms".
Russian laser system announced by President Putin in 2018; its purpose has not been officially stated.
A body such as ASCAP, BMI, SESAC or Global Music Rights that licenses the public performance of songs to the business where the music is played.
Irreversible, uncorrectable, seriously disabling loss of vision: acuity below 20/200 Snellen in both eyes.
10^15 watts of peak power, held for only femtoseconds.
Heating tissue with light until it seals or dies; first used on the retina, with sunlight and arc lamps before lasers.
A sensor that turns light into an electrical signal; scanners and disc players use them to read reflections.
A light-activated drug plus light of a matching wavelength kills the cells that absorbed the drug.
The light-activated drug in photodynamic therapy, such as porfimer sodium.
A laser with pulses in trillionths of a second, used for tattoos and pigmented lesions.
A tiny pressed mark on a CD, DVD or Blu-ray that reflects light differently from the flat surface, encoding bits.
FDA's stricter review requiring clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness, used for LASIK and SMILE lasers.
The smallest thing laser software controls: an X position, a Y position, on or off, and usually a color.
One X-Y-color position sent to the projector. A frame is a list of them.
The condition lasing needs: more atoms in the excited state than in the ground state.
The weaker first laser shot that flattens a tin droplet before the main pulse turns it into plasma.
Reshaping the surface of the cornea with an excimer laser, without cutting a flap.
Form FDA 3632, the manufacturer's report on a laser product to FDA.
A named output area with its own size, position, geometric correction and safety settings.
The 1995 protocol to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons on blinding laser weapons, in force since 1998.
A yellow-light laser that targets blood vessels, used for port-wine stains.
The energy source that creates the population inversion, usually light or electricity.
A laser making very short, high-peak-power pulses in nanoseconds, used to break up tattoo ink and pigment.
Holding lasing back while gain builds, then releasing it as one intense pulse, typically nanoseconds long.
An image built from closely spaced horizontal lines, as on a TV; too fast for scanner mirrors beyond low resolutions.
A generally analog console that lets the laserist change size, position, color and effects live.
The firms named in an FDA import alert whose products can be detained without examination.
Vaporizing thin sheet with a high-intensity beam and no assist gas.
The connector US law requires on Class IIIb and IV laser systems; an emergency stop plugs into it.
Usually two facing mirrors that send light back and forth through the gain medium, turning an amplifier into an oscillator.
The first laser (1960): a pulsed red source at 694 nm. It flashes, so it was no use for drawing.
The standard an automated system must meet to replace human safety observers at an outdoor US show.
A person watching the airspace or beam paths who can terminate the beam immediately; ILDA's draft standard calls the role a laser spotter.
A safeguard that blanks the beam if the scanners stop moving it.
A system that cuts the beam if the scanning mirrors stop moving; listed by the UK HSE among standard controls for laser displays.
A feature that prevents exposure above the limits if the scanning mirrors slow or stop. Required on scanned laser products in the US by 21 CFR 1040.10(f)(9).
The 2013 FDA proposal's term for the control that would replace the key switch requirement.
Choosing a wavelength and pulse length so heat stays in one target - pigment, blood or ink - and spares the tissue around it.
What a laser company charges per day of show, worked out from equipment write-off, overhead and margin.
A mechanical flag inside the projector that blocks the beam ahead of the scanners; the beam attenuator of the US rule.
A laser treatment of the eye's drainage tissue that lowers eye pressure in glaucoma.
A femtosecond laser cuts a small disc inside the cornea, which the surgeon removes through a small incision.
An excited atom releasing light on its own, in a random direction.
The second person at a Laserium show, who followed a written script to time the house lights and the planetarium's star projector.
A passing photon makes an excited atom release a second photon matching it in wavelength, direction and phase.
The fractional change in length a gravitational wave causes; 10^-21 for the 2015 detection.
The laser that marks a target for a guided munition.
A track on Laserium's four-track show tape that helped new laserists learn the timing.
Distance equals half the round-trip time of a light pulse multiplied by the speed of light.
A running clock signal, such as SMPTE or MIDI timecode, that keeps lasers, lights, video and audio on one timeline.
The spacing between neighboring turns of a disc's spiral track, about 320 nm on Blu-ray.
On/off-only laser control, giving seven colors and no fades.
Unique Device Identifier; reusable, reprocessed US medical devices must carry it on the device itself.
The naked eye or eyes with ordinary corrective lenses, as Protocol IV uses the term.
A projector feature that lets the operator widen or narrow the beam during a show.
FDA permission to vary from a requirement of a performance standard - for shows, the 5 mW cap in 21 CFR 1040.11(c) - on stated safety conditions.
A requirement the FDA attaches to a variance approval, binding on the holder. The 3.0 m and 2.5 m audience separations are conditions.
Vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser, a tiny chip laser that emits from its surface, used in phone depth sensors.
A point with automatic sample placement: the software adds samples along long lines and at corners.
Images stored as points joined by lines and drawn as outlines.
Wavelength division multiplexing: sending several closely spaced laser colors down one fiber to multiply capacity.
A mixed argon/krypton ion laser that emits red, green and blue lines from one tube.
Drawing with one beam by steering it horizontally and vertically with two mirrors, the way an oscilloscope draws.
Software limits that keep beams out of set areas such as the audience, crew positions, balconies and glass.
